paragraphs.heading: A special subset
paragraphs.text: An ideal is a special subset of a ring. The model is a set like the even numbers, or the multiples of 3, inside the integers. Adding or subtracting two evens gives an even, and multiplying an even number by any integer, odd or even, also gives an even. These two features, closure and absorption, are what define an ideal.

paragraphs.heading: Quotients and kernels
paragraphs.text: An ideal lets you build a quotient ring, much as a normal subgroup lets you build a quotient group. An ideal I splits R into equivalence classes, and these classes form an abelian group written R/I, the quotient of R by I. The map sending each element to its class is a surjective ring homomorphism whose kernel is the ideal. In the other direction, the kernel of a ring homomorphism is always a two-sided ideal, so two-sided ideals are exactly such kernels.

paragraphs.heading: Left, right and two-sided
paragraphs.text: A left ideal is a left submodule of R, with R viewed as a left module over itself; a right ideal is defined the same way from the other side. An ideal that is both is two-sided. In a commutative ring the three notions coincide and one simply says ideal, and in the noncommutative case "ideal" often means two-sided. Every ideal contains the zero ideal and lies inside the unit ideal, which is R itself. An ideal other than the unit ideal is called proper, and a left ideal is proper exactly when it contains no unit element.

paragraphs.heading: Examples
paragraphs.text: The even integers form the ideal 2ℤ, and all integers divisible by a fixed n form the ideal nℤ. Every nonzero ideal of ℤ is generated by its smallest positive element, so ℤ is a principal ideal domain. Real polynomials divisible by x² + 1 form an ideal in ℝ[x]. Among n × n matrices, those whose i-th row is zero form a right ideal, while those whose j-th column is zero form a left ideal but not a right one.

paragraphs.heading: Ideals in place of numbers
paragraphs.text: In the integers, ideals match the non-negative integers one-for-one, since each ideal is the multiples of a single such number. In other rings the ideals need not match the elements so directly, and some properties of integers carry over more naturally to ideals than to elements. Prime ideals play the part of prime numbers, and the Chinese remainder theorem extends to ideals. In a Dedekind domain, a kind of ring important in number theory, ideals have a version of unique prime factorization.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name comes from
paragraphs.text: Ernst Kummer invented ideal numbers to act as the missing factors in number rings where unique factorization breaks down. Here "ideal" meant existing only in imagination, like points at infinity in geometry. In 1876 Richard Dedekind swapped Kummer's undefined notion for concrete sets of numbers that he named ideals, in the third edition of Vorlesungen über Zahlentheorie, a book by Dirichlet. David Hilbert and especially Emmy Noether later carried the idea to polynomial rings and other commutative rings.
